explain: Cosines are bounded by 1. With s = 1 and 3 classes, even the best case (cosine 1 to the true class, -1 to the others) gives p = 0.787. Scaling by s lets the probabilities approach 1 so the cross-entropy can be driven down.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
question: Which setup best measures a function that in production runs once per request on cold data?
options: Many iterations on one small input with a long warm-up
Many iterations, each preceded (outside the timed region) by touching a buffer larger than the last-level cache, with batching to amortize pause overhead
One iteration, measured once
Many iterations on a single input with ASLR (address space layout randomization) disabled
explain: Evicting the caches before each timed call recreates the cold state, and batching keeps the PauseTiming overhead small relative to the work. A long warm-up measures the hot case. A single run is dominated by noise and timer overhead. ASLR, which places the stack, heap and libraries at random addresses on each run, affects layout, not cache warmth.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
question: A harness re-serializes tool-call arguments (same JSON object, different whitespace) on every turn. Under the strict matcher, a linear session keeps rolling back. What is the narrowest fix the docs offer?
options: --session-message-matcher loose_tool_call
--session-message-matcher role_content_only
Pass --apply-chat-template so the harness renders the prompt
Set input_ids yourself in each request
explain: loose_tool_call accepts equivalent JSON-object argument representations while still requiring call IDs, function names and order to match. role_content_only would also work but can merge genuinely different tool histories. The docs say not to apply the chat template manually or set TITO control fields like input_ids.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Learned indexes: a model that predicts where a key lives
question: A single-model learned index stores min error -3 and max error +2. What is the worst-case number of binary-search probes inside the window, compared with binary search over all 12 keys?
options: 1 probe versus 12
3 probes versus 4
6 probes versus 12
2 probes versus 3
explain: The window holds 2 + 3 + 1 = 6 slots. Binary search over n slots needs at most floor(log2 n) + 1 probes: 3 for 6 slots and 4 for 12. Probe counts scale with the log of the window, which is why shrinking error from thousands to tens matters more than shrinking it from 6 to 3.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
question: A mobile game sells in-game coins. The studio worries that players will modify the app to unlock paid items for free. Which MAS testing profile is aimed at that attacker?
options: MAS-L1, because other installed apps are the adversary
MAS-L2, because the operating system cannot be trusted
MAS-R, because the user of the device is the attacker
MAS-P, because coins are personal data
explain: MAS-R's attacker model is the device's own user, including reverse engineers and cheaters. L1 and L2 protect the user from other parties; P is about personal data. Note that R only slows cheaters down: the coin balance itself must still live on the server.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Dynamic instrumentation with Frida: watch and change a running app
question: A tester has a stock, non-rooted Android phone and wants to use Frida on a client's app. Which statement is right?
options: Injected mode works the same; frida-server needs no special rights
It is impossible; Frida needs root in every mode
Frida can only instrument iOS apps without root
They can use embedded mode: package Frida Gadget into the app and re-sign it, which changes the app's signing identity
explain: Without root, ptrace into another app's process is not allowed, so injected mode fails. Embedded mode puts the gadget inside the app; the repackaged app must be re-signed with a different key, which is also something servers and integrity checks can notice (lessons 2 and 12).

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: WebViews: a browser inside the app, with a bridge to native code
question: In the TikTok chain, which single change would *not* by itself have broken the attack?
options: Stopping the redirect handler from forwarding to internal deep links
Making the host filter impossible to bypass
Restricting the bridge to TikTok's own origin
Making the App Link use a custom scheme instead of https
explain: Swapping the https link for a custom scheme would not help: any app or page can still trigger a custom-scheme link, and it adds hijacking risk. Each of the other three removes a link in the chain: reaching the WebView, loading the attacker's page, or the page reaching privileged methods.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Running a mobile app assessment end to end, and where to practise
question: Which finding is best fixed on the server rather than in the app?
options: A WebView bridge exposed to all frames
An event-bound biometric check
An exported activity forwarding nested intents
A 'hide my distance' setting that the API ignores, returning precise distances anyway
explain: The distance is in the API response, so any client receives it; only the server can stop sending it, and that fix protects every app version immediately. The other three are client bugs on the device, fixed by app updates (and, for the bridge, also by what the server lets the WebView load).

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Decoupled RoPE: why position breaks absorption
question: Why is the decoupled RoPE key $k^R_t$ shared across all heads, while the RoPE query $q^R_{t,i}$ is per head?
options: Keys must be cached and queries do not; sharing the key keeps the cache at $d_c + d_h^R$ instead of $d_c + n_h d_h^R$
Because RoPE only works with a single head
To save FLOPs on the query side
Because the latent already contains position
explain: Queries are computed for the current token only and discarded, so per-head queries cost no cache. A per-head key would add $n_h d_h^R = 8192$ elements per token per layer in DeepSeek-V3.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why MLA can beat GQA at equal cache, and converting models
question: Why must a converted model handle RoPE before it can use absorbed decoding?
options: Absorption only works with 64-wide heads
RoPE makes the cache larger than GQA's
With RoPE on every key dimension, a position-dependent rotation sits between the query and $W^{UK}$, so $W^{UK}$ cannot be folded into the query
The fine-tuning data has no position information
explain: This is lesson 4's problem again: $q^{\top} R_{j-t} W^{UK} c_j$ has a different rotation for every cached position. Confining RoPE to a small decoupled part leaves the rest absorbable.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading
question: Why did S-LoRA put adapter weights and KV cache in one paged pool instead of two separate pools?
options: Because both are stacks of H-sized vectors that come and go dynamically, so sharing H-sized pages avoids fragmentation and lets the split between them change with load
Because adapters and KV cache are always the same size
Because the base model weights also need paging
Because PCIe transfers require page-aligned buffers
explain: A KV tensor is (S, H) and a LoRA weight is (R, H). With pages of one H-vector each, both fit the same allocator, holes left by one can be reused by the other, and the balance shifts automatically between many adapters and long contexts.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
question: Your index stores 3 chunks per web page. Fusion is keyed by chunk id and the top-5 after RRF holds 3 chunks of the same page. What is the most direct fix?
options: Fuse by source document id (or collapse chunks of one page) before truncating to 5
Raise k from 60 to 600
Generate more paraphrases
Switch from RRF to an unranked union
explain: The slots are being spent on near-duplicates of one source. Keying fusion or a post-fusion collapse by source id frees slots for other documents. Changing k or adding phrasings does not address what counts as a duplicate.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
question: Under Wang, Lin and Metzler's cost model, you double k0 from 500 to 1000 in a BM25 plus monoBERT pipeline. What happens to monoBERT's cost per query?
options: It stays the same, because monoBERT runs once per query
It grows by about log 2
It roughly doubles, because cost is unit cost times the number of documents scored
It quadruples
explain: monoBERT scores each candidate independently, so its cost is U x k0. Nogueira et al. report exactly this: latency increases linearly with the number of candidates, while quality shows diminishing returns.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: Your LLM listwise reranker on the top 100 meets quality targets but costs too much per query. Which change follows the cascade principle best?
options: Run the LLM on the top 100 but with a random initial order to avoid bias
Drop stage 1 and let the LLM read the whole corpus in windows
Let a distilled cross-encoder rerank the 100 and send only its top 20 to the LLM in one window
Increase the step size to 20 so windows no longer overlap
explain: Put the cheap model where the list is long and the expensive model where it is short: one LLM window instead of 9 calls. RankGPT's own GPT-4-on-top-30 result follows the same pattern. Random initial order hurt in the paper, and s = w removes the overlap that carries good passages forward.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-V3: sequential MTP modules with a full causal chain
question: Why did the DeepSeek-V3 ablation conclude that MTP improved the model itself rather than just adding capacity?
options: The MTP models had more active parameters at inference
The module was discarded at inference, so the evaluated networks had identical cost and shape
MTP models were trained on more tokens
Only benchmarks that MTP helped were reported
explain: During evaluation the MTP module is dropped, so baseline and MTP models run the same main network at the same cost. The difference comes from how the shared weights were trained. The table even includes a regression (MMLU at large scale).

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
question: Why is full-matrix AdaGrad not used for a $4096 \times 4096$ linear layer?
options: Its preconditioner has about 2.8 x 10^14 entries (around 1.1 PB in fp32), far beyond any accelerator's memory
It diverges on non-convex losses, so it only works for linear models
It needs the Hessian, which backpropagation cannot provide
It ignores correlations between parameters, so it is no better than Adam
explain: The preconditioner is $mn \times mn$ with $mn \approx 1.68 \times 10^7$, so it has about $2.8 \times 10^{14}$ entries. It uses gradient outer products, not the Hessian, and it captures *all* correlations; the problem is purely size and the $O(m^3 n^3)$ cost of its inverse root.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
question: In SOAP, what happens if you force $Q_L = I$ and $Q_R = I$ for a layer?
options: The layer is trained with plain Adam
The layer is trained with Muon
The layer is frozen
The layer is trained with full-matrix AdaGrad
explain: With identity rotations, $G' = G$ and SOAP's inner step is an ordinary Adam step in the original coordinates. That is exactly what the paper does on very large sides such as the vocabulary dimension: it skips the rotation there because an $m \times m$ eigenbasis would be too costly.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
question: A paper compares its optimizer to AdamW at the halfway checkpoint of a run with cosine learning-rate decay and reports 1.8x fewer steps to reach AdamW's halfway loss. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing, as long as both runs used the same batch size
Mid-run, neither learning rate has finished decaying, and loss curves can cross during the decay, so the ranking at the end may differ
Speedups must be measured in FLOPs, never in steps
Cosine decay is not allowed for second-order optimizers
explain: Wen et al. show loss curves of different optimizers crossing several times while the learning rate decays, so intermediate checkpoints can mislead. Compare at the end of each run's planned budget, ideally across several budgets. The unit matters too, but steps are a legitimate unit if reported as such.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
question: Your model ties the input embedding and output unembedding weights. Which muP formulation from the paper fits best?
options: Table 3, because it is the main table
Neither; muP cannot be used with tied embeddings
Table 8, which gives input and output weights the same init and LR scaling and puts a 1/fan_in multiplier on the logits
SP with a smaller global learning rate
explain: Table 3 initializes output weights with variance $1/\text{fan\_in}^2$ but input weights with $1/\text{fan\_in}$, which conflicts if they are the same tensor. Table 8 is an equivalent formulation where all vector-like parameters share one rule and the width factor moves into a forward multiplier, so tying works. `MuSharedReadout` implements this.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Transferring across depth: branch multipliers, Depth-muP, CompleteP
question: Under CompleteP ($\alpha = 1$) with AdamW, you go from a 2-block proxy to a 32-block target at the same width. What happens to the residual branch multiplier and to the hidden-weight LR?
options: Multiplier 1/16, hidden LR divided by 4
Multiplier 1/16 (L/L_base = 16), hidden LR unchanged, since $L^{\alpha-1} = L^0$
Multiplier 1/4, hidden LR unchanged
No change to either; CompleteP only affects width
explain: CompleteP multiplies each branch by $(L/L_{base})^{-1} = 1/16$ and scales AdamW block LRs by $(L/L_{base})^{\alpha - 1} = 1$. Depth-muP ($\alpha = 1/2$) would instead use multiplier 1/4 and divide the block LRs by 4.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
question: A waiter calls `FUTEX_WAIT(&word, 2)`, but by the time the kernel checks, `word` is 0. What happens?
options: The call returns immediately with EAGAIN and the thread does not sleep
The thread sleeps until the next FUTEX_WAKE
The kernel sets the word to 2 and then sleeps
The kernel wakes all other waiters on the word
explain: FUTEX_WAIT only sleeps if the word equals the expected value at the moment the kernel checks it. A mismatch means the state changed since the caller decided to wait, so it returns EAGAIN and the caller retries in user space.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
question: Your app does `SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id = 7`, computes stock minus 1 in code, then `UPDATE items SET stock = <computed>` in the same Read Committed transaction. Two requests run this concurrently on stock = 5. What can happen?
options: Both requests block forever in a deadlock
Final stock is 3, because Read Committed serializes the updates
The second UPDATE fails with error 40001
Final stock is 4: one decrement is lost
explain: Both SELECTs can see 5, both compute 4. The second UPDATE waits for the first, then writes the constant 4 onto the new version. Fixes: write `SET stock = stock - 1`, lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or use Repeatable Read and retry on 40001.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The task: pull typed spans out of running text
question: Why did the memorisation baseline reach precision 71.91 percent but recall only 50.90 percent on the CoNLL-2003 English test set?
options: Entity names are rare in newswire, so there was little to memorise
Names are an open class and the test set is from a different month, so a dictionary of training phrases matches only about half of its entities
The baseline used the wrong tag set and so could not represent multi-token spans
Precision and recall are measured on different entity types
explain: Train and dev are August 1996 Reuters news, test is December 1996. New stories mean new names, and a dictionary cannot find a name it never saw. When it does fire it is often right, which is why precision is much higher than recall.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Transformer taggers and subword alignment
question: You fine-tune a BERT tagger and score 94 F1 on your own eval but 89 when a colleague scores the same predictions. The only difference is that you evaluated on WordPiece tokens and they evaluated on words. Why can your number be higher?
options: WordPiece tokens are easier to classify than words
You scored a different gold sequence, since masked continuation pieces and specials change the entity set and the counts
Scoring on pieces double counts true positives but not false positives
The discrepancy means the alignment code is broken
explain: The metric counts spans over whatever unit you give it. Pieces and words are different sequences with different entity boundaries, so the two runs are measuring different problems. Only the word-level number is comparable to published results.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Picking blocks: importance scores come for free
question: A teammate proposes letting each of the 16 heads in an NSA GQA group keep its own top-16 blocks, arguing it is more accurate. What is the main cost?
options: The backward pass becomes non-differentiable
Decoding would load the union of up to 256 blocks per group instead of 16, losing most of the memory savings
Compression would no longer work
The window branch would have to grow to compensate
explain: Heads in a group share KV, so separate selections are loaded as a union. With 16 heads x 16 blocks that can be up to 256 distinct blocks. Summing scores over the group and taking one top-16 keeps reads at 16 blocks while every head uses all of them.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Where NSA sits: fixed patterns, routing, MoBA and InfLLM-v2
question: A team adds MoBA-style block selection to a dense GQA model with 8 query heads per KV head, each head choosing its own top-4 blocks by mean-pooled keys. Decode latency barely improves. What should they change first?
options: Use a larger block size
Replace mean pooling with an MLP
Make the heads of each group share one selection, for example by summing or averaging their block scores as NSA and InfLLM-v2 do
Turn off the forced current block
explain: Decoding is memory bound, and heads in a group share one KV cache, so independent picks load the union of up to 32 blocks. Summing (NSA) or averaging (InfLLM-v2) scores over the group and taking one top-4 keeps loads at 4 blocks. Block size and scoring function do not fix the union problem.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
question: With 64-bit hashes, m = 4 substrings and threshold r = 7, what is the per-substring search radius that guarantees no match within 7 is missed?
explain: floor(7/4) = 1. If all four substrings differed by 2 or more, the total would be at least 8 > 7, so some substring differs by at most 1. Using 0 could miss pairs such as 2+2+2+1; using 7 is correct but wastes thousands of probes per table.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: The three contracts: policy, generation and environment interfaces
question: Why do generation backends in NeMo RL exchange token ids rather than strings with the trainer?
options: Token ids compress better over NCCL
vLLM cannot return text
Strings cannot be stored in a BatchedDataDict
So the trainer and the inference engine can never disagree because of different tokenizer versions or settings
explain: The generation design doc says backends process tokens directly without involving the tokenizer, which removes inconsistencies between tokenizer versions or specifications in the two frameworks. The log-probs the trainer recomputes are then for exactly the tokens that were sampled.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN
question: Your office uses only switches, no hubs. A colleague says sniffing is therefore impossible on the office LAN. What is the best reply?
options: Wrong, because switches copy every frame to a monitoring port by default
Wrong: broadcasts and unknown destinations are flooded, table overflow can force flooding, and ARP or DHCP tricks can redirect frames to an attacker
Wrong, but only for Wi-Fi users
Correct: switches send each frame only to its destination port
explain: Switching reduces what a sniffer sees but does not stop a local attacker. Flooding, MAC table overflow and redirection attacks all deliver other people's frames to the attacker's port. Mirror ports exist but are configured by administrators, not on by default.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Kaminsky 2008: poisoning a whole domain
question: Why did Kaminsky's attack use names like www12345678.bank.example instead of www.bank.example?
options: A name that is not cached forces a new query to the real server at once, so the attacker can race again immediately instead of waiting for a TTL
Random names are shorter, so forged packets are smaller
Random names bypass bailiwick checking
Resolvers do not check query IDs for random names
explain: The whole speed-up comes from always asking for an uncached name. Each one opens a fresh window, so attempts are limited only by how fast the attacker can send, not by record TTLs.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: SYN floods and SYN cookies
question: Why do SYN floods usually use spoofed source addresses, and why does that matter for SYN cookies?
options: Spoofed sources never send the final ACK, so their entries sit in the backlog; with cookies there is no entry, and no ACK means no work
Spoofing makes packets smaller; cookies need small packets
Spoofed addresses bypass the firewall; cookies re-enable it
Spoofing is required by TCP; cookies remove the requirement
explain: The flood works because each SYN creates state that waits for an ACK that never comes. SYN cookies create no state, and the only thing that creates a connection is a correct ACK, which a spoofing attacker never sees the SYN-ACK to compute.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Scanning, as defenders see it
question: A closed port and a filtered port are probed with a SYN. How do they differ in Zeek's conn.log?
options: Closed: history S, state S0. Filtered: history Sr, state REJ.
Closed: history Sr, state REJ. Filtered: history S, state S0.
Both show ShR
Zeek does not log either
explain: A closed port answers with RST (lower-case r, from the responder), which Zeek records as REJ. A filtered port gives no answer at all, which is S0, a connection attempt with no reply.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Packets, flows and logs: three kinds of network evidence
question: A team wants to detect a workstation uploading 5 GB to an unknown server at night, across 4,000 hosts, cheaply, and keep a year of history. Which evidence fits best?
options: Flow records or Zeek conn.log, which record bytes per connection
Full packet capture on every link, kept for a year
Suricata alerts only, since a rule will match the upload
Wireshark running on the analyst's laptop
explain: Volume questions need byte counts per connection, which flows and conn.log record in a few hundred bytes per connection. A year of full packets for 4,000 hosts is enormous. A Suricata rule only fires if someone wrote a rule for this traffic, and a laptop running Wireshark sees only its own traffic.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: From overview to stream: the Wireshark workflow, decryption and tshark
question: A stream to TCP port 8443 shows in Wireshark only as 'Data', but the bytes start with 'GET /update HTTP/1.1'. What is the right next step?
options: Use Decode As to dissect TCP port 8443 as HTTP, then read the requests
Conclude the traffic is encrypted
Delete the packets because Wireshark cannot read them
Re-capture with a larger snapshot length
explain: Wireshark chose no HTTP dissector because 8443 is not a port it maps to plain HTTP and no heuristic matched. The payload is plainly HTTP, so Decode As fixes the dissection. The user guide gives the same example with HTTP on port 800.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: What TLS still reveals, and fingerprinting clients with JA3
question: Why does JA3 drop GREASE values before hashing?
options: Browsers insert randomly chosen GREASE values, so keeping them would give the same browser a different fingerprint on each connection
They are encrypted and cannot be read
GREASE values only appear in server hellos
RFC 8701 forbids logging them
explain: GREASE (RFC 8701) reserves values like 0x0a0a that clients add at random to keep servers tolerant of unknown values. They carry no information about the client, and keeping them would make one browser look like many. The JA3 README says it ignores them so programs that use GREASE still produce a single hash.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: DNS as a control channel: tunnels, generated names and SUNBURST
question: Your Zeek sensor sits on the internet link, outside the internal DNS resolver. A DNS tunnel runs from one workstation. What does dns.log show as the client?
options: The internal resolver's IP address, because the resolver makes the outbound query on the client's behalf
The workstation's IP address
The attacker's IP address
Nothing, because Zeek ignores recursive queries
explain: The workstation asks the internal resolver, which asks the internet. A sensor outside sees only the resolver's queries, so every tunnelled name appears to come from it. Log at the resolver itself or monitor the client side to attribute queries to hosts.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Layers: the OSI and TCP/IP models, and why both exist
question: A vendor sells a 'layer 7 firewall'. What can it do that a firewall that only reads IP addresses and ports cannot?
options: Block traffic from a list of IP addresses
Inspect the application protocol, for example tell a normal HTTP request from one with an attack string in it
Forward Ethernet frames between switch ports
Encrypt the traffic between two offices
explain: Layer 7 is the application layer, so the device parses HTTP, DNS and so on. Blocking by IP address is a layer 3 job any packet filter can do; forwarding frames is layer 2 switching; encrypting between offices is a VPN.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
question: traceroute shows the routers on the path to a host. Which mechanism makes each router reveal itself?
options: Routers answer a special 'who are you' broadcast
Each probe has a TTL one higher than the last; the router where it reaches zero sends back ICMP time exceeded from its own address
BGP announcements list every router on the path
The destination host sends back a list of routers it was reached through
explain: TTL is a hop counter for loop protection. A router that decrements it to zero must drop the packet and may send an ICMP time exceeded message, whose source address is the router itself. traceroute raises the TTL step by step to collect one router per step.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTP: requests, responses, headers and cookies
question: A session cookie is set with `HttpOnly` but not `Secure`, and the site is also reachable over plain HTTP. What risk remains?
options: Scripts in the page can read the cookie
The cookie is sent to every other website
None, HttpOnly covers both cases
The browser may send the cookie over an unencrypted connection, where anyone on the path can read it
explain: HttpOnly only hides the cookie from page scripts. Without Secure, the browser will include it on plain http:// requests to the site, and those cross the network in clear text. Set both, and serve the site only over HTTPS.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
question: A server allocates a large buffer pool at startup and fills it from a single loader thread. Benchmarks show workers on node 1 are slower than workers on node 0. Which change fixes placement with the least code?
options: Call malloc from each worker thread instead of the loader
Add a read-only warm-up pass on each worker after loading
Increase the size of the pool so it spans both nodes
Have each pinned worker write its own share of the pool during startup
explain: Placement happens on the first write, not on malloc and not on a read (a first read of anonymous memory maps the shared zero page). Having each pinned worker write its share first puts those pages on the worker's node.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
question: numastat shows numa_miss = 0 and numa_foreign = 0 on every node, yet threads on node 1 see slow memory. Which explanation fits?
options: Allocations were local to the allocating thread, but the pages are used by threads on another node
The counters are broken on this kernel
Node 1 has no memory, so its CPUs never miss
explain: numastat counts where allocations were satisfied relative to the allocator's preference. A single initializer thread produces perfect counters while the consumers on node 1 read remotely. Check /proc/PID/numa_maps for page locations.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
question: A database deletes old SSTable files (the sorted, immutable data files a log-structured merge tree writes and later replaces during compaction) but the file system is mounted without discard and fstrim never runs. What happens inside the SSD?
options: Nothing changes: deleted files free their flash pages automatically
The FTL still considers those LBAs live, so cleaning keeps copying dead data and write amplification rises
The drive becomes read-only
The data is erased immediately to free space
explain: Deleting a file only updates file system metadata. Until the LBAs are trimmed (deallocated), the drive must preserve their contents and copies them during every cleaning of their blocks.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
question: Two detectors have the same AP at IoU 0.5, but detector X has much higher AP@[.5:.95]. What does that tell you?
options: X finds more objects
X is faster
X has fewer classes
X's boxes are more tightly aligned with the ground truth
explain: At IoU 0.5 both find and rank objects equally well. The stricter thresholds (up to 0.95) only reward detections whose boxes overlap the truth very closely, so X's advantage is localization precision.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
question: New writer B (epoch 2) tries its fencing write at WAL slot 2 and gets 412. Reading slot 2, it finds an SST from old writer A with epoch 1. What should B do?
options: Halt, because it lost the race
Overwrite slot 2 without a condition, since its epoch is higher
Retry the fencing write at slot 3
Wait for A's lease to expire, then retry slot 2
explain: This is RFC-0001's second example. A simply got one more SST in before B's fence. Because the winner's epoch is older, B moves to the next ID and retries; once its fence lands, A will hit B's SST and halt. Halting is only right when the winner's epoch is newer. Overwriting would destroy A's acknowledged data.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
question: You must report the fraction of requests served under 300 ms, and you want to be able to change that threshold later without redeploying the service. Which instrument?
options: A histogram with a boundary at 0.3, since stored bucket counts let the server compute any threshold that has a boundary
A summary configured with quantile 0.95
A gauge set to the duration of the last request
A counter incremented whenever a request finishes under 300 ms
explain: The counter answers today's question exactly but hard-codes 300 ms into the binary. The summary fixes the quantiles, not a threshold, at instrumentation time. The gauge throws away every request but the last. Only the histogram keeps counts you can query differently later, limited to the boundaries you chose.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
question: A greedy CTC decoder sees the argmax path  - - c c - a a - t t - t  (with - as blank). What does it output?
options: cat
catt
ccaatt
catat
explain: Merge repeats first: - c - a - t - t. Then drop blanks: c a t t. The blank between the two t groups keeps them as separate characters.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The reference monitor: one checker that sees every access
question: To save time, a file server remembers "alice may read report.pdf" for an hour after the first check. Alice is removed from the project after five minutes. Which principle does the cache weaken?
options: Separation of privilege
Open design
Complete mediation
Economy of mechanism
explain: Complete mediation says every access is checked against the current policy, and Saltzer and Schroeder warn specifically about remembered results. For 55 minutes alice keeps access they no longer have.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Linux capabilities: splitting root into pieces
question: Ana's shell has empty permitted, inheritable and ambient sets. Ana runs a binary whose file capabilities are cap_net_raw=p (permitted only, effective bit off). Which capabilities are in the new effective set right after execve?
options: All capabilities, because it is a privileged file
CAP_NET_RAW and CAP_SETUID
None: the file effective bit is off, so the new permitted capability is not raised automatically
CAP_NET_RAW
explain: P'(permitted) is {NET_RAW}, but P'(effective) equals P'(permitted) only when the file effective bit is set; otherwise it equals P'(ambient), which is empty. A capability-aware program can raise NET_RAW itself later with capset.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Namespaces and cgroups: the building blocks of containers
question: Which statement about containers is accurate?
options: cgroups hide other containers' processes
Each container runs its own kernel
Namespaces give a private view and cgroups limit resources, but all containers on a host share the host kernel
A PID namespace stops kernel bugs from being reachable
explain: Views come from namespaces, limits from cgroups, and the kernel is shared. That shared kernel is why lesson 13 looks at gVisor and microVMs.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Secure boot, module signing and kernel hardening knobs
question: What does `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1` prevent?
options: All use of gdb
Root from debugging anything
A compromised process from attaching to unrelated processes of the same user, such as an SSH agent, to read their memory
Core dumps
explain: Under classic rules any process can ptrace other dumpable processes of the same UID. Mode 1 limits attachment to descendants (or explicitly declared debuggers), while CAP_SYS_PTRACE still allows admins to attach.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: What OSINT is, and what it is for
question: Public information becomes intelligence, in the statutory definition, when it...
options: is collected and delivered to address a specific requirement in time to be useful
is classified by a government agency
comes from at least three independent sources
is gathered with automated tools
explain: The definition ties intelligence to timely delivery to an appropriate audience for a specific requirement. Classification, source counts and automation are not part of it.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
question: Why is the GHDB useful to a defender?
options: It lists categories of exposure to search for on your own domains and fix
It patches Google's index
It blocks dork queries against your site
It contains your organisation's leaked passwords
explain: Its categories (password files, sensitive directories, error messages) are a checklist of what should never be indexed. It does not change search engines or block anyone.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
question: Your best match fits three of four clues, but a building visible in the video is missing from the satellite image. What is the right next step?
options: Declare the match, since three of four is strong
Discard the candidate immediately
Ignore the building as noise
Check the imagery date; if the building is newer than the imagery, look for more recent imagery to confirm
explain: Imagery age is a known failure mode. A missing building can mean the wrong place or old imagery; resolve which before deciding. Declaring or discarding without checking are both premature.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Bulk collection and its ethics: the Parler archive (2021)
question: Parler's posts were public. Why was the design still a security failure?
options: Public posts should never be visible to anyone
Predictable IDs and no rate limits let anyone copy everything, including location metadata, in bulk
The posts were encrypted badly
The two-factor authentication gave administrators away
explain: The issue was enumerability at scale plus metadata. Wired reported the administrator-hack rumour was false; public visibility of individual posts was intended.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CMake in three phases: configure, generate, build
question: After a first configure with GCC, you run `CXX=clang++ cmake -S . -B build`. The build still uses GCC. Why?
options: CMake only reads CXX on Windows
Ninja caches the compiler path in .ninja_log
clang++ must be passed with -G
The C++ compiler was fixed in CMakeCache.txt on the first configure and cannot be changed in that build tree
explain: CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER is chosen on the first configure of a build tree (from CXX or -D) and the docs say it cannot be changed afterwards. Use a new build directory or cmake --fresh.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
question: A job in your fork PR fails at a step that uploads benchmark results using `secrets.BENCH_TOKEN`. The same job passes on the maintainers' pushes to `main`. Why?
options: Secrets other than `GITHUB_TOKEN` are not passed to runners for workflows triggered from forks
Fork PRs run on slower runners, so the upload times out
Secrets expire after each push
The workflow file in your fork is ignored
explain: The GitHub docs state that, with the exception of `GITHUB_TOKEN`, secrets are not passed to the runner when a workflow is triggered from a forked repository, and that token is read-only there. This protects the project from PRs that try to exfiltrate secrets.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
question: Your PR adds a feature, and an unrelated-looking test `test_download_retry` fails in CI once. Which response is best?
options: Add `@pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=5)` to the test in your PR
Push an empty commit until CI goes green
Run the node id locally on the merged branch; if it passes, check whether it also fails on `main` or other PRs and mention that evidence in the PR
Set `fail-fast: false` in the workflow
explain: Gather evidence before labelling a failure flaky: reproduce on the merged code, then look for the same failure without your change. Silencing or repeatedly re-running a test you may have broken is exactly how real regressions get merged.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: GitHub mechanics: decisions, suggestions and merge rules
question: Your PR was approved, then you pushed one more commit fixing a typo in code. The repository requires reviews and has stale review dismissal on. What happens?
options: The approval stays because the change was small
The PR merges automatically
The approval is dismissed and the PR needs a new approval before merging
GitHub reverts your commit
explain: With required reviews and stale review dismissal enabled, any code-modifying commit pushed to an approved PR dismisses the approval. GitHub does not judge whether the change was small.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
question: An LLVM issue is labelled `good first issue`. You can fix it in two minutes with a coding agent and you will carefully review the result. Is that allowed under LLVM's policy?
options: Yes, as long as you review the output and add Assisted-by
Yes, but only if a maintainer approves the agent first
No, because LLVM bans all AI tools
No: AI tools must not be used to fix good first issues, which exist as learning opportunities
explain: LLVM generally allows tools with a human in the loop, but makes a specific exception: AI tools must not be used for issues labelled good first issue, since automating them squanders the learning opportunity.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
question: You want to fix a typo in the *message* of an earlier commit without changing any code, and let autosquash apply it. Which command creates the right commit?
options: `git commit --fixup=<commit>`
`git commit --squash=<commit>`
`git commit --fixup=reword:<commit>`
`git commit --amend`
explain: `--fixup=reword:` creates an `amend!` commit that replaces the target's message and ignores staged changes. Plain `--fixup` keeps the target's message. `--amend` only rewrites the latest commit, not an earlier one.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
question: Which change to a proprietary app is most likely to pull it under GPL-3.0 terms when shipped?
options: Calling a GPL-3.0 command-line tool through a pipe
Putting a GPL-3.0 tool on the same installer as a separate program
Statically linking a GPL-3.0 library into the app's executable
Reading a file format that a GPL-3.0 program also reads
explain: Code in the same executable is one program in the FSF's view, and GPLv3 section 5(c) then covers the whole work. Pipes and aggregates keep programs separate, and a file format is not code you copied.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
question: Besides numbers that back up a claimed gain, what else does the kernel's patch guide ask for in an optimization patch?
options: A link to a third-party benchmark website
Proof that the gain holds on every architecture Linux supports
A description of the non-obvious costs and expected downsides, so the reviewer can weigh them
Nothing else: numbers alone are sufficient
explain: The guide says optimizations usually trade CPU, memory and readability, or one workload against another, and asks you to describe the expected downsides so the reviewer can weigh costs against benefits.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches
question: Which GitHub code search query finds where Redis **defines** a function named lookupKeyRead?
options: `repo:redis/redis lookupKeyRead`
`symbol:lookupKeyRead`
`repo:redis/redis symbol:lookupKeyRead`
`repo:redis symbol:lookupKeyRead`
explain: symbol: matches definitions and repo: scopes to one repository. repo: needs the full owner/name, since partial repository names are not supported. A bare term matches any file whose content or path contains it, so the first query returns every call site too.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
question: You remove a block of logging setup and the program no longer fails at all. What does this tell you?
options: The logging setup is part of what triggers the bug, so it must stay in the repro (perhaps in a smaller form)
Nothing; flaky programs sometimes pass, so delete the block anyway
The bug was in your logging code, so it is not worth reporting
explain: If the failure disappears when a piece is removed, that piece is needed to trigger it. Put it back and try to shrink it rather than delete it. It does not prove the bug is in your code. If you suspect flakiness, rerun several times before concluding anything (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
question: Which PR is most likely to be flagged as too large, according to Google's guidance?
options: A 200-line bug fix in one file
A change that only deletes three obsolete files (900 removed lines)
A 200-line change spread across 50 files
A 60-line change with 40 lines of tests
explain: Size includes spread. The guide says a 200-line change in one file might be okay, but across 50 files it would usually be too large. Deleting whole files counts as roughly one line each, and tests belong in the change.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
question: A kernel reads the KV of position `pos` at `base + pos * bytes_per_token`, as a contiguous kernel would. After switching to paged storage, what goes wrong?
options: It reads the right tokens only while the sequence fits in its first block; later positions land in whatever block happens to sit next in memory
Nothing, because physical blocks are allocated in increasing order
It reads correct data but more slowly
It fails only for requests that share blocks
explain: Logical blocks are mapped to arbitrary physical blocks (7, 1, 3 in the example). Only offsets inside a block are contiguous, so every access must go through the block table: `table[pos // B] * B + pos % B`.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
question: A client asks you to test their online shop, which runs on a large hosted e-commerce platform. The client has signed your permission to test. What is still missing?
options: Nothing: the client's signature covers everything the shop uses
Checking the platform's own security testing policy, because the client cannot authorise testing of the provider's systems
A faster scanner
Permission from the shop's customers
explain: PTES: the client does not speak for third-party providers. Many platforms publish testing rules or bug bounty scopes; only what they allow can be tested, and only the client's own parts.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: certificate logs, search engines and leaked code
question: A team issues individual certificates for `vpn`, `jira-test` and `payroll-old` under their domain. What does Certificate Transparency mean for them?
options: Nothing, because certificates are private between the CA and the company
Those names are permanently in public append-only logs, so each host must be secured as if everyone knows it exists
The names are hidden unless someone guesses them
CT only logs expired certificates
explain: CT logs are public and append-only, and Chrome requires publicly trusted certificates to be logged. Anyone can search them, so obscure names give no protection.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Web enumeration: crawling, content discovery and fingerprinting
question: During discovery `/admin/` returns 403 and `/admin-old/` returns 404. What do you report?
options: Both paths exist
Neither path exists
/admin/ exists and refuses access (worth checking whether it is meant to be reachable at all); /admin-old/ appears not to exist
/admin-old/ is hidden better and is more dangerous
explain: 403 means the server knows the resource and refuses it; 404 means it found nothing (unless the app masks codes). An admin path reachable from the internet, even if refusing, is worth reviewing.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Attack surface management: recon as a defender
question: Which control would most directly have prevented a server from becoming one of the 32,820 wiped MongoDB databases?
options: A stronger ransom-negotiation policy
Encrypting the database files on disk
A longer password on the operating system's root account
Not exposing port 27017 to the internet and enabling MongoDB access control, verified by an external scan
explain: The attacks needed only network reachability and no authentication. Disk encryption does nothing against a logged-in database client; binding locally, firewalling and enabling auth do.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
question: In a flame graph, `json_encode` is 300 px wide but the boxes on top of it cover 290 px. What does that tell you?
options: json_encode itself is the hot spot; optimize its loop
json_encode was called 300 times
Almost all of json_encode's time is in the functions it calls; it executes very little itself
json_encode ran during the first quarter of the profile
explain: Only the exposed top edge (10 px) is self time. The other 290 px belong to its callees. Width says nothing about call counts, and x position says nothing about when.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
question: Spot the bug: `n->key = k; n->next = old; clwb(n); head = n; clwb(&head); sfence();` (n fits in one line; head is in another line).
options: Nothing: the final sfence orders everything before it
CLWB should be CLFLUSH, because CLWB keeps the line in cache so it is not durable
The sfence must come between clwb(n) and head = n; otherwise head can be durable before the node
head must be written with a non-temporal store
explain: The single trailing fence only guarantees both lines are durable at the end. Before it, head = n may be evicted or written back first, giving the head-only crash state. CLWB keeping a clean copy in cache is fine: the data was written back.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
question: IC3 2025 shows about 191,561 phishing complaints and 24,768 BEC complaints, but BEC losses are about 14 times larger. What best explains this?
options: Phishing is often the entry step, while BEC is where large wire transfers are lost
BEC victims exaggerate their losses
Phishing has stopped causing any losses
BEC complaints are counted in a different currency
explain: Phishing is the common first step: it steals passwords or opens conversations. BEC is the monetising step, where a single fraudulent wire can be millions. The categories overlap, so the totals are a rough picture, not exact accounting.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Envelope, header and display name: why spoofing works
question: Why can receiving servers not simply reject every message whose envelope-from differs from its header From?
options: Because SMTP forbids comparing them
Because the header From is encrypted
Because envelope-from is always empty
Because mailing services legitimately use their own bounce address while sending as a brand's From address
explain: Bulk senders, ticketing systems and forwarders routinely use a different envelope-from to collect bounces. DMARC solves this with alignment rules that allow related domains instead of demanding an exact match everywhere.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Reading headers to triage a suspicious message
question: A message has two Authentication-Results headers: the top from mx.corp.example (dmarc=fail) and a lower one from mx.corp.example (dmarc=pass). Which do you trust?
options: The lower one, because it is older and closer to the sender
The top one, because it was added by your border server on arrival
Neither; Authentication-Results are always forged
Both; take the more favourable
explain: Your border server prepends its result on arrival, so the top one carrying your own authserv-id is yours. Anything lower was written before your server got the message. RFC 8601 says such forged copies should be deleted by the border server.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing and why passkeys resist it
question: After an AiTM incident, the help desk resets the victim's password. Why is that not enough?
options: Passwords cannot be reset remotely
The attacker's stolen session cookie may stay valid until sessions are revoked
The attacker also needs the new password to keep reading mail
Password resets delete the mailbox
explain: The attacker never needed the password after login; the cookie is the access. Revoke sessions and tokens, remove attacker-added MFA methods and inbox rules, then reset.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
question: What is `sizeof(union U)` for `union U { char s[13]; int i; };` on x86-64?
explain: A union's size is its largest member, 13 bytes for s, rounded up to the union's alignment, which is 4 because of i. 13 rounded up to a multiple of 4 is 16. 17 would add the members instead of overlapping them.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Strict aliasing: which pointer casts C lets you read through
question: Which of these reads of `double d = 2.0;` is defined behavior in C?
options: `unsigned char b0 = *(unsigned char *)&d;`
`long bits = *(long *)&d;` (both 8 bytes, alignment 8)
`int lo = *(int *)&d;`
`float f = *(float *)&d;`
explain: Character types may read any object, so reading one byte of d through `unsigned char *` is fine. long has the same size and alignment as double here, but size and alignment do not matter to the aliasing rule: only the types on the list in 6.5 paragraph 7 may read a double.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
question: A C library takes `double` arguments in meters. You wrap them in Rust as `struct Meters(f64);`. Which attribute guarantees a `Meters` is passed exactly like an `f64`?
options: #[repr(C)]
#[repr(transparent)]
#[repr(packed)]
None: a one-field struct is always passed like its field
explain: repr(transparent) gives the struct the layout and ABI of its single non-zero-sized field. repr(C) promises C struct layout, but the Reference notes a C struct's ABI can differ from the bare field's; the default repr promises nothing.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
question: A squat-depth checker flags every rep as too shallow, but only for users who film from directly in front. What is the most likely cause?
options: The OKS sigma for knees is too large
Foreshortening: in a frontal 2D view the thigh points at the camera, so the 2D knee angle looks straighter than it is
The heatmap resolution is too low
Hysteresis thresholds are too far apart
explain: A 2D angle measures the projection. When thigh or shin points toward the camera, it shrinks in the image and the projected angle opens up (111 degrees in 3D looked like 173 in the example). OKS sigmas only affect evaluation.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
question: Why did NIST select HQC in March 2025 when ML-KEM was already standardised?
options: HQC is faster and smaller than ML-KEM
Because HQC is the only KEM approved for hybrids
Because ML-KEM was broken
As a backup based on different math (error-correcting codes), in case a weakness is found in ML-KEM
explain: NIST's announcement calls HQC a second line of defence and says ML-KEM remains the recommended choice. Cloudflare's 2025 review adds that HQC is larger and slower on every metric, so it is insurance rather than a replacement.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: KyberSlash: when one division leaks the key
question: Which deployment was most exposed to KyberSlash?
options: A browser doing hybrid TLS with a fresh key share per connection
A laptop verifying ML-DSA signatures
A server that only encapsulates to clients' keys
An embedded device with one long-term Kyber decapsulation key that decapsulates ciphertexts from anyone on the network
explain: The attack needs many timed decapsulations under the same secret key. Ephemeral TLS keys block that; a static key reachable by attackers does not.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Rolling it out: browsers, middleboxes and big certificates
question: Roughly how many extra bytes would ML-DSA-44 add to the authentication part of a first TLS visit (5 signatures, 2 public keys), compared with ECDSA P-256?
options: About 1.5 kB
None: signature sizes are similar
About 150 kB
About 15 kB
explain: 5 x 2420 + 2 x 1312 = 14,724 bytes versus about 450, so roughly 14 kB more. This is the 'second migration' problem that Merkle Tree Certificates aim to solve.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
question: An engineer says: pre-filtering is always exact, so it is always better than post-filtering. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, exactness always wins
Pre-filtering cannot handle AND conditions
Its flat-scan cost is s n distances, which at broad filters is close to a full scan; post-filtering a graph search is far cheaper when most vectors match
Pre-filtering returns fewer than k results when s is small
explain: Exactness is not free. At s = 0.6 on 50 million vectors, a flat scan does 30 million distance computations, while post-filtering loses little (60% of candidates survive) at graph-search cost. Pre-filtering never under-fills: it returns k whenever at least k vectors match.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
question: You move a linked-list walk to a CPU with twice as many fill buffers. The list nodes are in random order. Roughly how does the walk's speed change?
options: About the same
About 2 times faster
About half as fast
Faster only if the list fits in L1
explain: A single pointer chase has concurrency 1: the next address is unknown until the current miss returns. Extra fill buffers sit empty. To benefit you would need several independent chains walked at the same time.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
question: Under GDPR Recital 26, which dataset is still personal data?
options: A published national count of all runners per year
Weather records with no link to people
A dataset of one person's data that was deleted
A table where names were replaced by random user numbers, with the mapping kept in another database
explain: Pseudonymised data that can be attributed to a person using additional information (the mapping) is still information on an identifiable person. National yearly counts and weather do not relate to an identifiable person.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: k-anonymity: generalise and suppress until you hide in a crowd
question: A table's equivalence classes have sizes 7, 5, 12 and 3. What k-anonymity does it satisfy?
options: k = 27, the total
k = 7, the first class
k = 3, the smallest class
k = 12, the largest class
explain: k is the guarantee for the worst-placed person, so it is the size of the smallest equivalence class: 3.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy in real systems: units, trust and hazards
question: A DP analytics product counts page views per day at epsilon = 1, treating each page view as the unit. One user views a sensitive page 50 times a day. What is the effective protection for that user's daily total?
options: epsilon = 1, as advertised
Stronger, because the user is lost in many views
Zero risk, because counts are aggregated
Much weaker: by group privacy about 50 x epsilon = 50, unless contributions are bounded
explain: Event-level privacy protects one view. Fifty views from one person behave like a group of 50, so the bound becomes about 50 epsilon. Bounding views per user per day restores a user-level guarantee at the cost of more noise.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Private set intersection: comparing lists without sharing them
question: In the DH-PSI protocol, why can the server not learn Ana's contacts from H(x)^a?
options: Because H(x)^a is encrypted with TLS
Because the server deletes the values
Because SHA-256 cannot be inverted
Because it can hash any guessed number, but comparing H(guess) with H(x)^a needs Ana's secret a, and finding a from the values it sees is a discrete logarithm problem
explain: The server could hash every phone number, but it cannot compare those hashes to H(x)^a without knowing a. That is the difference from plain hashing, which a server can test guesses against.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a privacy review, and where to practise
question: A partner asks for 'anonymised' per-user listening histories to build a recommender. Which response best follows this course?
options: Hash user IDs and send the histories
Avoid releasing records: offer DP aggregates, or let the partner's code run in a controlled environment on your side
k-anonymise the histories at k = 5 and send them
Remove names and send a 10 percent sample
explain: Sparse behavioural histories are re-identifiable even without identifiers (Netflix), hashing is reversible on known IDs (lesson 3), k-anonymity fails on high-dimensional data, and sampling did not help Netflix. Releasing no records is the robust option.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 3: setuid, capabilities, kernel bugs, docker group
question: Your patch tool reports that the fixed kernel for Dirty Pipe was installed yesterday. `uname -r` shows the old version. What is the state of the host?
options: Protected: the package is installed
Protected only for new processes
Still vulnerable: the old kernel is the one running until a reboot or live patch
Partly protected: half the kernel is updated
explain: The kernel in memory is the one that booted. Installing a new kernel package changes files in /boot, not the running code. Until the host reboots into it, or a live patch is applied, the bug is still there.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Credentials are the real currency: where they live on a host
question: CISA found NotPetya also infected fully patched Windows machines. What made that possible?
options: Credentials stolen from memory were reused with built-in admin tools (WMIC, PsExec)
EternalBlue worked on patched systems too
It exploited a zero-day in Windows Update
Patched machines had SMBv1 re-enabled
explain: EternalBlue only worked against unpatched SMBv1. The modified Mimikatz plus WMIC or PsExec route needed no vulnerability, just valid credentials, so patching did nothing to stop it.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Defending the path: segmentation, admin hygiene, EDR, HSE timeline
question: PwC found several detections in the HSE network weeks before the ransomware ran. What was the main failure?
options: There were no security tools at all
The attacker used an unknown zero-day exploit
Logs were encrypted by the ransomware before anyone could see them
Detections did not lead to an investigation and response in time
explain: Antivirus saw Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on 31 March, hospitals saw alerts in May, and a provider flagged unhandled threats the day before. None became an incident investigation in time. Where the Department of Health did act, the ransomware was largely prevented.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Step labels without humans: Monte Carlo rollouts
question: A step is mathematically correct, but its soft-estimation label is 0.125 (1 of 8 rollouts succeeded). What is the best explanation?
options: The step is subtly wrong; SE is never low for correct steps
Soft labels are always one eighth of hard labels
The completer rarely finishes this hard problem correctly, so SE measures the policy's success chance, not step correctness
The reference answer must be wrong
explain: SE is a Monte Carlo value estimate for the completer's policy. On a hard problem even correct prefixes rarely finish well. This is the PRM-versus-value-model confusion the Qwen team identified.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Generative PRMs: verifiers that reason before they judge
question: A team wants a step-level verifier for best-of-16 reranking on olympiad math and has only a few thousand step labels. Which choice fits best?
options: A long-CoT generative verifier fine-tuned on filtered verification chains, accepting the higher cost per verification
A discriminative PRM trained on the few thousand labels
Hard-estimation MC labels with N = 64 to remove noise
Product reduction of an ORM's scores
explain: ThinkPRM reached strong ProcessBench F1 from about 8K step labels by starting from a reasoning model and training it to write verification chains. A discriminative PRM needs far more labels, and more MC rollouts make hard labels more optimistic (lesson 4), not cleaner.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step
question: Two threads of the same process alternate on one CPU. Compared with two separate processes alternating, which step does the kernel skip?
options: Saving and restoring the general-purpose registers
Switching kernel stacks
Loading a new page table root (CR3 on x86) and the TLB work that comes with it
Running the scheduler to pick the next task
explain: Each thread still has its own registers and kernel stack, so those are always swapped, and the scheduler always runs. Only the address space is shared, so switch_mm finds the same mm and returns without touching CR3.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
question: A logging thread receives each log line from 16 worker threads through a mutex-protected queue and is woken for every line. At 200,000 lines per second, `voluntary_ctxt_switches` on the logger is enormous. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Give the logger a higher scheduling priority
Use more logging threads, one per worker
Batch: let workers append to a buffer and wake the logger once per batch (or every few milliseconds) instead of per line
Pin the logger to core 0
explain: Each line wakes the logger, which handles it and sleeps again: one voluntary switch per line on the logger, plus wakeup work for the workers. Batching turns 200,000 handoffs into a few hundred. More logging threads multiply the switches, and priority or pinning do not change how often they happen.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Code size vs recall, and refinements: OPQ, fast scan, ScaNN
question: A 4-bit fast-scan index (PQ32x4fs) and an 8-bit index (PQ16) both use 16 bytes per vector. Which statement matches the Faiss docs?
options: Fast scan is faster but less accurate than 8-bit PQ at the same memory, so pair it with re-ranking
They are identical because the bytes are equal
Fast scan is more accurate because it has more sub-quantizers
Fast scan stores float32 tables in registers
explain: Faiss notes 4-bit PQ is less accurate than 8-bit PQ for the same memory and recommends a refine stage. Its speed comes from 16-entry tables quantized to 8-bit integers, which fit in SIMD registers.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse
question: A colleague scores 64 OPRO candidates on 30 dev examples and reports the winner's 93% as the expected production accuracy. What is the best response?
options: Accept it: OPRO uses temperature 0 for scoring, so scores are exact
Accept it if the winner is shorter than the baseline
Ask for the winner's score on a held-out set, and use a larger validation set; with 64 candidates and 30 examples the winner's dev score is strongly inflated
Re-run OPRO with temperature 1.0 for the scorer
explain: Temperature 0 makes each score repeatable, not accurate: 30 examples still give a standard error near 0.05 per prompt, and the best of 64 is inflated by more than 2 standard errors in the equal-accuracy model. Only an untouched held-out set gives an unbiased estimate.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: A residue is a rigid frame: rotation plus translation
question: Gram-Schmidt subtracts the e1 component from the CA to N vector before normalising. What would go wrong if you skipped the subtraction and just normalised both bond vectors?
options: The matrix would still be a rotation, since both vectors have unit length
The determinant would be negative instead of positive
The third axis would be undefined because the cross product of unit vectors is zero
The two columns would not be orthogonal (the bond angle is 111.3 degrees, not 90), so R would not be in SO(3) and would distort distances
explain: Unit length is not enough: a rotation matrix needs orthogonal columns. The N-CA-C angle is about 111 degrees, so the two normalised bond vectors are not perpendicular, and a matrix built from them would stretch and shear instead of rotate.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores
question: A script decodes each log line with `errors="strict"` (the default). One line in a million contains the byte 0xff. What happens?
options: That line is skipped automatically
The byte becomes a question mark
A UnicodeDecodeError stops the script unless you catch it
Python guesses another encoding for that line
explain: Strict decoding raises `UnicodeDecodeError` on invalid bytes. Unless you catch it (lesson 4) or use `errors="replace"`, the run ends at that line and the rest of the log is never checked.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
question: Which statement about base64 is true?
options: It encrypts data with a fixed key built into the standard
It compresses data so it fits in URLs
It makes data about one third larger, turning every 3 bytes into 4 characters
It can only encode text, not binary files
explain: Base64 carries 6 bits per character, so 24 bits (3 bytes) need 4 characters: roughly 33 percent growth. There is no key and no compression, and it was designed precisely for arbitrary binary data.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Safe coding habits: no eval, no shell strings, no secrets in code
question: A colleague loads a config with `rules = eval(open("rules.txt").read())` because the file looks like a Python list. What should replace it?
options: exec instead of eval
pickle.loads
ast.literal_eval, or better, store the rules as JSON and use json.loads
eval with a try/except around it
explain: literal_eval accepts only literal values, so a function call in the file is refused with ValueError. JSON is even better because other tools can read it too. Wrapping eval in try/except does nothing: the injected code runs before any exception could happen, and pickle and exec have the same problem.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: Rocchio, pseudo-relevance feedback and RM3
question: RM3 with fbDocs = 10 hurts a query whose first-pass results contain only 1 relevant document in the top 10. What is the most direct fix?
options: Raise fbTerms so more terms dilute the bad ones
Lower the original query weight to 0.1
Use fewer feedback documents or a higher original query weight, or skip PRF when first-pass confidence is low
Switch the first pass from BM25 to TF-IDF
explain: The expansion terms come from the assumed-relevant documents. With 9 of 10 off-topic, more terms or a lower original weight make drift worse. Fewer feedback docs, more weight on the original query, or not applying PRF to this query limit the damage.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Rewrite-Retrieve-Read: training a rewriter on the reader's feedback
question: Why does the reward include a Hit term (+1 if the answer string appears in the retrieved text, -1 otherwise) besides EM and F1?
options: It directly rewards retrieving useful evidence, even when the reader fails to use it
It replaces the KL penalty
It makes the reward differentiable
It penalizes long queries
explain: EM and F1 depend on the reader as well as the query. Hit isolates the rewriter's own job, getting the answer into the retrieved context, so a good query is rewarded even if the frozen reader misreads the passage.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Binary search plus rescoring: oversample, then re-rank
question: Your binary index is in RAM and original vectors are on an SSD. Recall is too low at oversampling 2. What is the main cost of raising oversampling to 8?
options: The binary index gets 4x larger
Queries must be re-embedded
Stage 2 reads about 4x more original vectors from disk per query
The Hamming scan must use floating-point math
explain: The binary scan cost barely changes. Stage 2 work, mostly random SSD reads of original vectors, grows with the number of candidates, so going from 2k to 8k candidates is about 4x more reads.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Extended RaBitQ, and binary quantization in real systems
question: You must serve 1536-dimensional embeddings with over 95% recall and cannot keep float vectors anywhere (no RAM, no disk) for rescoring. Which option fits best?
options: 1-bit binary quantization with oversampling 8
Plain BQ with a Hamming-only ranking
1-bit RaBitQ with error-bound re-ranking
Extended RaBitQ with about 5 bits per dimension
explain: Every 1-bit option relies on re-ranking with stored originals to reach high recall. Extended RaBitQ was designed for this case: the paper reports B = 5 stably gives over 95% recall without raw-vector re-ranking.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Workflows as state machines: skipping, repeating and reordering steps
question: In Kettle's role-selection case, which design choice would have made the skipped page harmless?
options: Hiding the application links until a role is chosen
Starting each session with no privileges and granting the chosen role only when the role request succeeds
Redirecting to /role with a 302 instead of a 301
Using POST instead of GET for the role page
explain: The bug was a fail-open default: sessions began as admin and were downgraded later. Starting with nothing and adding privileges as each step completes means a skipped step leaves the user with less access, not more.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Flexcoin and Poloniex, the bitcoin banks that raced (2014)
question: Sirer argued the Flexcoin attackers "did not do anything they were not allowed to do". What does that imply for testing?
options: A test must send the allowed requests concurrently and check the invariant (no overdraft); per-request permission checks cannot see this bug
Authorization tests alone would have found the bug
Only code review can find race conditions
Two-factor authentication prevents race conditions
explain: Each transfer was permitted for that user, so any test that checks one request at a time passes. The bug only appears when the same allowed request runs many times at once, which is what a concurrency test does (lesson 13).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests
question: A team's test applies a coupon twice in a row and checks the second is refused. Which bug can this test never find?
options: A coupon redeemed twice by two requests that arrive at the same moment
A coupon accepted after its expiry date
A coupon applied to a product it was not meant for
A coupon code that is case-insensitive
